newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Swiss the losers if EU talks fail-Commission.
newsitem.headline: Swiss the losers if EU talks fail-Commission.

text.p: Switzerland risks losing more than European Union countries if talks on rail and road freight carriage through the Swiss Alps fail, a senior European Commission official told Reuters on Tuesday.

"The Swiss need the agreement more than the Community," the official said in reference to a range of linked EU/Swiss talks on closer research ties, free movement of workers, market access for farm goods, public works rules and technical trade barriers.

Last Friday, European Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock called off a meeting of EU transport ministers slated for next Thursday, saying Berne had reneged on an earlier offer in bilateral transit talks.

The official said that Swiss negotiators, by index-linking the average transit charge for trucks crossing their territory from 2005, risked adding up to 15 percent to the 460 Swiss franc ($326) figure mooted in earlier talks.
Swiss diplomats have refused to respond to Kinnock's claims, saying only that Berne's offer remained on the table and that Switzerland remained determined to go on with talks.
The Commission official was not so reticent.
"As far as we are concerned, we have gone as far as we can, it's for them to review their position. They will have to make up their mind whether they want a deal or not.

"Many member states and frankly the Commission as well, feel that there are other priorities which are moving up the agenda. The fact is that the file could go into suspension for a couple of weeks or months," the official said.
France and Austria, meanwhile, face increased traffic on their Alpine passes due to Switzerland's 28-tonne truck-weight limits and its curbs on heavy-goods road transit traffic.
Vienna also faces the Commission's legal challenge to its increased truck tolls on its Brenner Pass link to Italy, although the official played down this problem.

"We are confident that even in the absence of a deal with Switzerland, a compromise on Austria and France can be found," the official said, adding that the issue would come up during the regular meeting of EU transport ministers om June 17/18.
"The Swiss are overplaying their hand a little bit if they think the entire solution to Alpine transport lies in their hands," the official said.

Talks on all the issues are intended to fill the legal void left by Swiss voters' 1992 "No" to membership of the European Economic Area, a free trade area linking the EU with the members of the European Free Trade Association (EFTA).
Austria, Sweden and Finland, three of Switzerland's five EFTA partners, have since joined the EU, leaving the Alpine nation increasingly isolated. ($=1.41 Swiss francs)
